newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU set to struggle over future power balance.
newsitem.headline: EU set to struggle over future power balance.

text.p: How power should be wielded in a future European Union with as many as a dozen new members is set to be one of the most contentious issues facing EU leaders when they meet in Amsterdam to negotiate a new treaty.

At the heart of the debate is a struggle between large countries seeking to exercise their clout in the bloc's decision making and smaller countries seeking to ensure they are not consigned to second-class status.

There is also a widespread agreement that the bloc needs to be streamlined. For that reason, much of the discussion during the negotiations leading up to the summit next Monday and Tuesday has been dominated by fights over what to do.
Britain, sometimes allied with others, has fought to keep national vetoes in many of those areas where they still remain.
France has demanded that the number of commissioners be brought down to 10 from the current 20 and be left there no matter how many new members are brought it.
Small countries such as Ireland and Luxembourg have refused to countenance any move that could strip them of their commissioners, seen by the small countries as the guarantors of their rights.
EU officials expect the issues to be among the last agreed at the summit on Monday and Tuesday, but one of the bloc's traditional compromises is already taking shape.

Small countries are expected to win their fight to ensure that they have a commissioner, with the current number of 20 remaining until the first new countries come into the bloc sometime early in the next decade.
After that big countries with two commissioners may be asked to give one up. Once the number of countries reaches 20, with one commissioner each, the issue would be revisited.
Some large countries, notably France and Germany, are still holding out for the Commission to be capped at 20.

In exchange for retaining their commissioner, the small countries are expected to cede some extra voting power to the larger states in ministerial meetings -- allowing the bloc's heavyweights to recoup some of the power they have lost through the EU's most recent enlargements.
Other changes are expected to be modest and relatively uncontroversial since Britain's Conservative Party, a vehement opponent of majority voting, lost power.
Some national vetoes will be given up in non-sensitive areas and the European Parliament will be given a little more say in matters decided by majority vote.
